question: How is fuel injected into the TAE 125 engine's cylinders?

options.text: At high pressure directly into the cylinders, one injection nozzle per cylinder supplied by a common rail
By a carburetor mixing fuel and air before the intake manifold
By port injection into the intake manifold, one injector per cylinder
By a single injector shared between all cylinders via a distributor

explanation: Fuel is injected at high pressure directly into the cylinders. Each cylinder has its own injection nozzle, all supplied from the common rail.

question: How is pressure generated inside the common rail?

options.text: By gravity feed from the header tank above the rail
By a high pressure pump which receives fuel from a low pressure pump, both mechanically driven by the engine
By an electric high pressure pump powered from the main bus
By the turbocharger compressor pressurizing the fuel lines

explanation: A mechanically engine-driven high pressure pump generates rail pressure, fed in turn by a low pressure pump - both mechanically powered by the engine itself.

question: During normal operation, from which tank is fuel taken to supply the engine?

options.text: Whichever tank the pilot selects with a fuel selector valve
Both tanks simultaneously, in equal proportion
The MAIN tank (left wing) only
The AUX tank (right wing) only

explanation: Normally fuel is taken only from the MAIN tank in the left wing. There is no fuel selector valve to choose between tanks - the AUX tank instead feeds the MAIN tank via the transfer pump.

question: What happens to fuel that is delivered to the rail but not injected into the cylinders?

options.text: It is burned off through a bleed injector
It is stored in a small accumulator until the next start
It is vented overboard through a dump valve
It is led back through the AUX tank into the MAIN tank, cooling the rail and warming both tanks

explanation: Surplus fuel is routed back through the AUX tank to the MAIN tank. This return flow cools the hot fuel leaving the rail while warming the cooler fuel sitting in both tanks.

question: Under what two conditions does the electrical fuel transfer pump switch itself off automatically?

options.text: When the auxiliary tank is empty or the main tank is full
When the ECU is switched to ECU B, or after 30 minutes of continuous running
When the fuel temperature exceeds 75 degrees C, or the airplane exceeds 129 KIAS
When the emergency fuel valve is set to OFF, or the gearbox exceeds 120 degrees C

explanation: The transfer pump is designed to stop automatically either when the AUX tank runs empty or when the MAIN tank becomes full, preventing overfilling.

question: If fuel transfer with the electric transfer pump becomes impossible, how can fuel still reach the engine from the AUX tank?

options.text: By selecting ECU B, which draws directly from the AUX tank
Fuel can be taken directly from the AUX tank, with the return line still transferring it toward the MAIN tank
It cannot - the AUX tank has no other connection to the engine
By opening the alternate air source, which cross-feeds the tanks

explanation: If the transfer pump path fails, fuel can still be taken directly from the AUX tank; because the return line always leads to the MAIN tank, fuel continues to move from right to left.

question: What is used to control rail pressure?

options.text: The power lever position directly, with no electronic control
The turbocharger waste gate valve
An electrical valve, using the return flow as its control parameter
A mechanical relief valve set to a fixed pressure

explanation: Rail pressure is controlled by an electrical valve that uses the fuel return flow as its parameter.

question: What are the three positions of the emergency fuel valve?

options.text: LEFT, RIGHT and OFF
NORMAL, CROSSFEED and OFF
ON, STANDBY and OFF
NORMAL, EMERG. TRANSFER and OFF

explanation: The emergency fuel valve on the center console has three positions: NORMAL, EMERG. TRANSFER and OFF, reached by turning the handle while pulling up its safety catch.

question: At what pressure does the MAIN tank's relief pressure valve operate, venting fuel and air to the outside?

options.text: 150 mbar (2 psi)
300 mbar (4 psi)
75 mbar (1 psi)
500 mbar (7 psi)

explanation: One of the MAIN tank's two vents includes a relief pressure valve operating at 150 mbar (2 psi), protecting the tank against overpressure if a transfer failure overfills it.

question: What is the function of the check valve with capillary fitted to the fuel tank vents?

options.text: It measures the rate of fuel consumption
It allows air to enter the tank but prevents fuel from flowing to the outside
It allows fuel to flow out but prevents air from entering
It filters solid contaminants from vented air

explanation: The check valve with capillary lets air into the tank as fuel is consumed, while preventing fuel from escaping outward; the capillary itself equalizes air pressure during climb.

question: Where is the gascolator located in the fuel system?

options.text: Inside each wing tank, above the coarse filter
In the engine compartment, next to the high pressure pump
At the lowest point of the fuel system, centrally on the fuselage underside near the wing leading edge
At the highest point of the fuel system, near the fuel cooler

explanation: A gascolator sits at the lowest point of the fuel system, fitted centrally on the fuselage underside about 30 cm forward of the wing leading edge, with its own drain valve.

question: Why can't the fuel quantity remaining be calculated by simple proportion from the AED's fuel quantity counts?

options.text: The AED only updates its reading once every 10 minutes
The probe measures volume, not mass, and fuel density varies too much
The counts only reflect the transfer pump's runtime, not tank contents
The capacity probe's indication is non-linear

explanation: The capacity probe's indication is non-linear, so neither proportional calculations of remaining fuel nor direct fuel-consumption calculations from the AED counts are possible.

question: With the Long Range Tank installed, what replaces the filler tube of the main and auxiliary tank?

options.text: Another tank chamber, of approximately 5 US gal (19 liters) capacity
A second gascolator with its own drain valve
A larger capillary vent system
A second capacity probe wired to the AED

explanation: The Long Range Tank option adds another chamber of about 5 US gal (19 liters) in place of the standard filler tube, while the venting system remains unchanged.

question: What is the purpose of the fuel cooler, and where does it draw its cooling air from?

options.text: It cools the ECU electronics, drawing air from the cabin ventilation system
It reduces fuel temperature in the return line between the AUX and MAIN tanks, drawing air through a scoop on the lower stub wing surface
It cools the engine oil, drawing air from the intercooler duct
It reduces coolant temperature, drawing air from the propeller slipstream

explanation: The fuel cooler, fitted between the main spars of the right stub wing, reduces the temperature of the fuel returning from the AUX to the MAIN tank, using cooling air from a lower-surface air scoop.

question: What operating principle does the alternate mean for fuel quantity indication (dipstick-style gauge) rely on?

options.text: Ultrasonic measurement through the wing skin
A calibrated dipstick inserted through the filler neck
Communicating containers, read from a vertical ascending pipe against the tank drain
A float switch connected to an electrical gauge

explanation: The device works on the principle of communicating containers: pressed against the tank drain and held against the stall strip at the wing leading edge, it shows fuel quantity on a vertical ascending pipe.

question: For an accurate reading, on what kind of surface must the airplane be standing when using the alternate mean for fuel quantity indication?

options.text: A slight nose-down slope
A slight nose-up slope
Any surface, since the device self-levels
Horizontal ground

explanation: The airplane must stand on horizontal ground for the alternate fuel quantity device to give an exact indication.

question: Where is the fuel quantity measuring device (alternate mean of fuel indication) normally stowed?

options.text: In a bag on the rear side of the pilot seat
In the baggage compartment
Clipped inside the front canopy
In the glovebox behind the instrument panel

explanation: Its designated storage place is a bag on the rear side of the pilot seat.

question: Between what temperatures does the lower yellow bar of the fuel temperature indication flash, marking the range in which the engine must not be started on Diesel Fuel or an uncertain blend?

options.text: -30 degrees C to +4 degrees C
-30 degrees C to -6 degrees C
-5 degrees C to +4 degrees C
-20 degrees C to 0 degrees C

explanation: The flashing lower yellow bar spans -30 degrees C to -6 degrees C, the no-start range on Diesel Fuel; between -5 degrees C and +4 degrees C the same bar is steady on instead, meaning take-off is not permitted.

question: If the airplane is operated with JET Fuel, is operation permitted while the fuel temperature indication is in the yellow range?

options.text: Only during cruise, never during start or take-off
Only if the Long Range Tank is not installed
Yes, operation in the yellow temperature range is permissible with JET Fuel
No, the yellow range is prohibited on any fuel grade

explanation: Unlike Diesel Fuel or an uncertain blend, JET Fuel operation is permitted in the yellow fuel temperature range.

question: Which of the following is an approved fuel grade for the DA 40 D, listed alongside Jet A-1?

options.text: AVGAS 100LL
MOGAS 95
AVGAS 91/96UL
JP-8 (MIL-DTL-83133)

explanation: Approved grades include JET A-1, JET A, JP-8, JET Fuel No. 3, TS-1 (with MÄM 40-256) and Diesel Fuel (EN590) - never an AVGAS or MOGAS grade, which would be wrong for a diesel-cycle engine.

question: In which two countries is the use of Diesel Fuel specifically not approved for this airplane?

options.text: Indonesia and Malaysia
Germany and Austria
The United States and Canada
France and the United Kingdom

explanation: A limitation specifically excludes Diesel Fuel use in Indonesia and Malaysia.

question: Why can solid particles forming in cold Diesel Fuel be a problem for this engine?

options.text: They are filtered automatically by the intercooler
They can block the gascolator filter, which is not heated
They dissolve the injector nozzle coating over time
They cause the fuel cooler baffle to jam shut

explanation: Cold Diesel Fuel can form solid particles that block the gascolator filter; since that filter is not heated, this risk is specifically called out for cold-environment operation.

question: Changing from Diesel Fuel operation to JET Fuel operation in a cold environment, how must each tank be refilled to ensure no diesel blend remains (Long Range Tank not installed)?

options.text: Topped off once to full capacity with JET Fuel
Drained completely and refilled with exactly 14 US gal of JET Fuel
Refilled at least twice with more than 10.6 US gal (40 liters) of JET Fuel each time
Refilled once with any quantity of JET Fuel

explanation: Each tank must be refilled at least twice with more than 10.6 US gal (40 liters) of JET Fuel - or 17.2 US gal (65 liters) with the Long Range Tank - otherwise both tanks must be drained before refueling with JET Fuel.

question: What is recommended to be recorded in the airplane log each time fuel is added?

options.text: The ambient temperature at refueling
The exact tank quantities before and after refueling
The fuel supplier's name
The fuel grade used

explanation: Because the fuel grade determines which temperature limitations apply, it is recommended to log the fuel grade at each refueling.

question: What must be checked in each tank during the pre-flight walk-around by draining a sample?

options.text: Water and sediment
Fuel temperature
The transfer pump's operation
The relief valve setting

explanation: Each wing tank drain is opened during the walk-around to check for water and sediment, drained until no water comes out.
